note: The registries the governance clauses read. This file is DATA — it changes when packages, surfaces or owners change. The clauses that read it are CODE (scripts/lib/governance-model.ts) — they change only by founder ruling on architecture. Nothing here is a per-pair verdict; verdicts are derived.

roles.note: A package's role comes from the `workspaces` glob in the root manifest that claims it — never from matching its directory path (Ruling 5). Adding a role folder is an edit here plus an edit to `workspaces`, and nothing else.

containment.note: A service lives inside exactly one layer. A layer belongs to itself. Composition roots live outside the tree and are the only actors permitted to reach across it.

surfaces.note: Who may name this surface. `everyone` = any actor; `composition roots` = the roles above plus the repo root; a list = exactly those roles or package names; an empty list = nobody.

framework/shared.why: the shared substrate — the one target every role may name

framework/db.why: the manifest-level dependency on the database package. Which surface INSIDE it you may touch is decided per surface below, so declaring the dependency is not itself a decision.

framework/api-contract.why: the request/response shapes two layers agree on. A service talks through its own layer, so it has no business naming the contract directly.

framework/design-system.why: there is exactly one user interface. A second consumer of the design system means a second interface, which is a product decision, not an import.

db:client.why: holding a database handle is not the same as touching a table

db:row-type.why: a row type is a shape, not an access path

db:bootstrap.why: putting the database into a known first-boot state is the job of whatever boots the system

db:schema-ns.why: one import that hands over every table at once. The database's own client factory does the same job for the one legitimate use.

db:unknown.why: an export of the database package that belongs to no named surface. Reaching it means the surface has not been decided yet.

db:testing.why: development code. A production file naming it is already an error under the production-may-not-name-development clause; this entry keeps the two answers from disagreeing.

db:util.why: ANOMALY, pending follow-up W1. escapeLikePattern, resolveAgentScaffoldSpecs and resolveProfile touch no database — no SQL, no schema, no connection. The surface should not exist. Ruling 12.3 moves them out; until then the founder's round-1 verdict stands for services and the researched verdict stands for everyone else.

endpoints.note: A door is dialled only if the target declares it.

httpApiLayers.why: a layer that publishes an HTTP API publishes it to the whole system. agent-execution is absent because it hosts no API.

mcpRouter.why: the router exists to serve the harness. Only the layer that owns the harness relationship, and the harness itself, dial it. It is mounted in the wrong place today — follow-up W3.

eventBus.why: the framework provides the bus. A framework package that also publishes on it is both the pipe and the water, and the bus can no longer be reasoned about from the outside.

rawRuntime.why: every model and harness call goes through one door so it can be recorded, priced and replayed. Constructing a vendor SDK anywhere else builds a path the rest of the system cannot see.

oneDoorSurfaces.note: The development world relaxes every production rule EXCEPT these. Each names a surface where production has exactly one door — going around it builds a world production cannot produce, which is the one thing a test may not do.
oneDoorSurfaces.why: a test may cross any boundary to arrange the world; it may not go around a door production has only one of
